title: Why Startups Switch to Hourly Recruiting: September 2026
summary: Contingency fees run 15% to 25% of salary. See how hourly fractional recruiting differs on cost, incentives, and visibility for startups. October 2026
body_markdown:
Contingency agencies typically charge a percentage of first-year salary, with any refund or replacement for an early departure depending on the agreement. Hourly[fractional recruiting](https://www.dover.com/) ties cost to time spent on the search, which can include deeper assessment of candidates who might grow with an early-stage team. This guide breaks down the cost and incentive differences between contingency and hourly recruiting, and why a startup might switch.


**TLDR:**


-


Contingency agencies typically charge a percentage of salary; hourly recruiting costs depend on the rate and time spent on the search.


-


Hiring quality includes performance and retention after the offer is signed; neither billing model guarantees long-term fit.


-


Hourly fractional recruiting uses rates set by each recruiter; any success fee or contract commitment depends on the agreement.


-


Can suit startups with several annual hires that need recruiting expertise but lack enough steady work for full-time recruiting headcount.


-


Some solutions act as the infrastructure layer fractional recruiting agencies are built on, with vetted recruiters and verified reviews from founders who have worked with them.


## The Hidden Economics of Contingency Recruiting


Contingency agencies typically calculate their[recruiter commission](https://www.dover.com/blog/startup-recruiter-commission-structures) as a percentage of first-year base salary, often 15% to 25%. For a $160,000 engineer, that’s roughly $24,000 to $40,000 per placement.[Indeed’s guide to headhunter fees](https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/finding-a-job/headhunters-fee) puts the average at 20% to 25%, and notes the percentage can run higher depending on the firm and the role.


The incentive difference runs deeper than price. Contingency recruiters typically get paid for a placement, with the payment trigger set by the agreement. That can put more weight on closing the search than on long-term fit, though replacement guarantees, repeat business, and reputation can also create incentives to support a successful hire.

## How Placement Incentives Can Affect Hiring Decisions


Payment tied to a placement can encourage speed over a closer assessment of fit, since a recruiter’s fee depends on making a hire. Recruiters working across multiple clients may submit candidates who meet basic job requirements but need more scrutiny for team fit and long-term potential, and that pressure can grow when multiple recruiters compete for the same role, unless the hiring team sets clear screening expectations.


Placement-based fees can leave a gap between the event that triggers payment and the long-term results your team cares about. If a hire leaves early, any refund or replacement depends on the agency agreement; the billing model alone does not determine retention.


## Hiring Quality Matters Beyond the Accepted Offer


[LinkedIn’s 2025 Future of Recruiting report](https://business.linkedin.com/hire/resources/future-of-recruiting) identifies new-hire retention and job performance ratings as common measures of hiring quality, and recommends structured interviews and job-related skills assessments to help teams judge candidates consistently. These findings support looking beyond a signed offer, but they do not show that contingency billing causes hiring failures or that hourly billing prevents them.[SHRM’s 2025 benchmarking reports](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) add context: among the SHRM members surveyed, only 20% of organizations track quality of hire.


Placement-based fees can create pressure to move candidates quickly, and when screening focuses mainly on resume credentials and technical question responses, factors relevant to long-term fit, such as team communication, startup risk tolerance, and ability to handle shifting priorities, can get less attention. Assessing these soft factors takes time, and competition for a placement fee can shorten that assessment, though the depth of screening depends on the recruiter and the agreed process.


## How Hourly Models Realign Recruiter Incentives With Startup Success


Hourly billing changes what you pay for. When[fractional recruiters charge for time](https://www.dover.com/blog/fractional-recruiter-hourly-rate-vs-agency-fees) instead of placement, you can budget for work beyond closing an offer, including deeper candidate assessment, with engagements covering sourcing through close under terms agreed upfront. Recruiters set their own rates, with any success fee or multi-month commitment depending on the agreement, and the agreed notice and cancellation terms determine when you can stop work if a recruiter doesn’t grasp your needs.


You can scale recruiting effort with actual hiring needs when the agreement allows it. Ramping three engineers this quarter? More hours may help. Paused hiring after your last round? Hours can fall too, subject to agreed minimums and notice terms.


## Transparency and Control: What You Gain with Hourly Billing


Hourly billing paired with shared activity tracking can give you visibility into who your recruiter contacts, which channels they use, and how candidates respond, so you can adjust mid-search if outreach isn’t working. A shared ATS supports that visibility: when the recruiter and hiring team keep the same pipeline up to date, the hiring manager can see sourcing activity, candidate stage, and outreach history without chasing status updates, duplicate outreach is easier to catch, and client-owned records stay with the company when the search ends.


Visibility depends on the working arrangement, not billing alone. Without shared tracking or agreed reporting, hiring teams may see candidate submissions without the sourcing context behind them, and multiple uncoordinated recruiters can mean duplicate or conflicting messages to candidates. A dedicated recruiter and shared process can help keep communication consistent under either billing model.


## When Hourly Models Make the Most Sense for Your Hiring Needs


Hiring volume helps determine your best recruiting approach, including how many people you need to bring on annually and whether you have existing recruitment infrastructure. If you’re hiring 1 to 2 people per year, you may not need ongoing recruiting support. Traditional agencies or fractional recruiters can both work at this volume, depending on role difficulty and budget, and the choice depends on whether you want to pay for a completed placement or for time spent on the search.


Hourly fractional recruiting can suit teams with several annual hires that need recruiting expertise but do not have enough steady work for a full-time recruiter. Fractional recruiters can support active searches, with hours reduced during quiet months under the agreed terms. The time needed to fill an engineering role depends on its complexity, the candidate pool, and the interview process.


As hiring grows, building internal capacity may become worth considering. A full-time recruiter provides dedicated capacity, though their bandwidth is still finite. Fractional recruiting can remain a fit when hiring comes in concentrated bursts instead of a steady flow, and the decision depends on workload, role complexity, and the cost of keeping recruiting headcount between searches.


Hiring software and recruiter capacity solve different problems. A free ATS can organize applicants, job postings, and interview feedback, but someone typically still needs to source candidates and run outreach. For a single, well-defined role with time to spare, software alone may be enough. When sourcing is stalling, the role is specialized, or founders are handling recruiting between other work, a fractional recruiter working inside the same ATS can add those hours while the hiring team keeps one shared record of the pipeline.


## What Changed in Startup Recruiting in 2026


When funding is tight, early-stage teams may prefer cost structures that scale down between hiring cycles, and hourly models can let teams reduce spend during slow stretches without ending the relationship, if agreed terms and the recruiter’s availability allow it. AI-assisted sourcing tools can support targeted outreach, but tool access alone does not replace recruiter judgment or relationships; clear activity reporting and costs that pause with hiring still depend on the agreement, not the billing model alone. On-demand fractional support can also suit searches a team wants to pause once a hire closes. Returning to the same recruiter can reduce onboarding work since context is already shared, though timing depends on availability and how much the role has changed.


### October 2026 Update: AI Oversight Belongs in the Recruiting Scope


For startups comparing recruiting models this October, AI oversight adds another consideration beyond fees.[Illinois’s AI hiring law](https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2024/10/illinois-becomes-second-state-to-pass-broad-legislation-on-the-use-of-ai-in-employment-decisions) took effect in January 2026, prohibiting discriminatory AI use in covered employment decisions and requiring notice of covered AI use, per[Seyfarth’s June legal update](https://www.seyfarth.com/news-insights/illinois-department-of-human-rights-temporarily-withdraws-proposed-rules-on-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-employment.html) . Proposed notice rules were temporarily withdrawn while the underlying law remained in effect, so teams hiring in Illinois may want counsel to check current guidance before setting their notice process.


That makes tool oversight a useful part of the recruiter agreement: which AI tools may be used, who reviews screening recommendations, and who handles required notices. With either billing model, clear responsibilities and human review matter alongside cost per hire.


## Making the Switch: What to Expect When Moving from Contingency to Hourly


You can test fractional recruiting on a single role while keeping current agency relationships intact, giving you useful side-by-side data without disrupting pipelines.


Onboarding may take a few days once role specs and the interview process are ready, and your recruiter can begin sourcing after scope and tool access are agreed.


A capped trial budget and clear cancellation terms can limit spending if the arrangement is not a fit, while better results may justify expanding the relationship.


## How Dover Supports Incentive-Aligned Recruiting for Startups


Dover describes itself as the infrastructure layer that fractional recruiting agencies are built on. The same shared ATS keeps candidate data client-side and outreach history visible to the hiring team in real time, whether a startup works with one dedicated recruiter or an agency running multiple searches. Recruiters in Dover’s network carry verified reviews so you can assess fit before engaging. Each recruiter sets their own rate, no long-term contract is required, and hourly, retainer, and pay-per-hire structures are all available.


Dover’s free applicant tracking system pairs with a $199/month Premium tier offering AI applicant scoring and AI note taking to support human review, so teams can track outreach and funnel performance from shared records. Hourly engagements carry no placement fee, while pay-per-hire engagements use a success fee. Candidate data stays with the company after every search, building a foundation each future hire can draw on.


## FAQs


### What should a startup check before choosing a free ATS?


Check whether the free tier expires, limits jobs and users, restricts access to older candidate records, or charges for reporting and data export. If you work with an outside recruiter, confirm guest access and permissions. If AI screening is available, treat it as support for review, with people still responsible for recommendations and hiring decisions.


### Do I need an ATS before bringing in a fractional recruiter?


No. A recruiter can start in your existing tools, such as Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, or a shared spreadsheet, and add sourcing, screening, and outreach capacity on top of your pipeline. Working in one shared system can give the recruiter and hiring team the same real-time view of candidate stages and outreach history, reducing status chasing and duplicate outreach. Agree upfront on where records live, who can access them, and how they transfer when the search ends. If you add a shared ATS later, allow time for setup and record transfer to preserve candidate context.


### What should a startup agree on before starting an hourly recruiting engagement?


Settle the hourly rate, a weekly or monthly hours cap, how hours get tracked and reported, and the notice and cancellation terms. Confirm whether any success fee applies, who owns candidate records and outreach history, and which tools the recruiter may use. If AI screening is part of the process, name who reviews its recommendations and who sends any required candidate notices. Terms vary by recruiter, so put them in writing before work begins.


## Final Thoughts on Recruiting Models That Actually Align with Startup Success


The difference between contingency and hourly recruiting starts with what triggers payment. One model pays for a placement; the other pays for time spent on the search. Neither guarantees long-term fit. The right choice depends on role difficulty, internal capacity, and how much search-cost risk the team is willing to carry. Dover’s[fractional recruiting](https://www.dover.com/) model, for instance, pairs a free ATS with on-demand recruiters as one way to put that approach into practice.
